newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibian budget seen focusing on medium-term goals.
newsitem.headline: Namibian budget seen focusing on medium-term goals.

text.p: Namibian Finance Minister Nangolo Mbumba is expected to focus on the country's medium-term economic strategy when he unveils his 1997/98 budget this week, local economists say.
But while social and industrial development spending will be high on his agenda, economists believe Mbumba will keep the country on track to reach its three percent deficit target by the year 2000.

"I think the Minister of Finance will appropriate more funds for the stimulation of industrial growth and urban development such as infrastructure in the communal areas," Rainer Ritter, economist at Ohlthaver & List, said.

Bank Windhoek economist Emile van Zyl said he expected Mbumba to direct most expenditure towards education, job creation and poverty alleviation -- key goals in Namibia's First National Development Plan.
"From a national development point of view I would like to see a larger portion of the budget going for capital projects and...the deficit before borrowing to be as small as possible," Van Zyl said.
He expected the budget deficit to come in at 4.5 percent of gross domestic product compared with an estimated 4.9 percent last year.

The country's public sector wage bill, one of the largest expenditure items in the past, was expected to remain the government's biggest headache despite recent recommendations for a leaner administration by the Wages and Salaries Commission.
Van Zyl said the public sector wage bill presented the government with a difficult problem.
"There's already a very high unemployment rate and the ability of the private sector to accommodate people will be limited because of the current downswing in the economic cycle," he said.
That downswing is expected to be countered by the recent good rains, raising hopes that the country will meet its five-year growth targets.
Nambian Economic Policy Research Unit senior researcher Dirk Hansohm said the rains made the development plan's five percent growth target feasible.

"We have been revising our previous growth estimate for last year from 2.5 percent to more than three percent on the basis of new figures on agricultural output, and if we had more than three percent even in a drought year it should be quite possible to achieve five percent in a normal year," he said.
Van Zyl noted that available revenue sources would continue to be under pressure due to the low economic activity and said improved rainfall this year would not free up funds from drought relief.

"You must remember that it did not rain food and cattle and there will be some time before the situation normalises in terms of production. So I think for this year at least, drought relief will still be in place," he added.

Revenues could be boosted by an increase in taxes as the country seeks to ward off the effects of lower receipts from the Southern African Customs Union (SACU), which groups South Africa, Lesotho, Swaziland, Botswana and Namibia.
"In the long-term our problem is the high dependence on the SACU revenue pool and I think Namibia cannot hope to get higher revenues from the renegotiation of the agreement," Hansohm said.
"In the face of trade liberalisation, we expect that revenue from tariffs will decline, so we will have to go more for other taxes, direct and indirect," he said.

Ritter said the business community was also looking for an announcement on the introduction of Value Added Tax (VAT) by 1999, a move which would do away with the present Sales Tax and Additional Sales Duty while broadening the tax base.
He said he hoped the government would make further progress on the privatisation front.
"I expect an announcement this year on NamWater in the budget -- that part of the Ministry of Water Affairs will become commercialised," he said.
Namibia's budget is scheduled to be presented to parliament at around 2.30 p.m. (1230 GMT) on Wednesday.
